title: GitHub Is Down
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        August 17, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Leon Neal/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            If you're struggling to access GitHub this morning, you aren't alone.
                                            GitHub appears to be down for users across the internet. Downdetector shows thousands of user reports as of Monday morning.
                                            The site will likely get back up and running shortly, assuming there are no larger issues behind the scenes.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're trying (and failing) to access GitHub Monday morning, you aren't alone. According to Downdetector, the hosting provider has over 15,000 user reports indicating issues or downtime with the service—up from roughly 3,000 reports when I first published this article. Whether you're a developer trying to update your repository, or you're a user trying to access one, GitHub may give you trouble. If the comments on Downdetector are any indication, this is not the first time GitHub has had service issues. One comment reads: "Cmon [GitHub] get your sh*t together...this is getting old." (The user added their own asterisks.) Scrolling through the comment history, users reported errors one or twice a week throughout August. I'm not a regular GitHub user, so I can't attest personally to repeated downtimes, but it does seem as though this isn't wholly unusual. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
As such, even though it isn't clear why GitHub is down right now, chances are good that the company will get the site up and running sooner than later. Assuming nothing catastrophic is happening behind the scenes, developers and users alike should be able to access the site sometime today. That said, as of 12:12 p.m. ET, the site is still having reported issues. I will continue to update this piece if GitHub's downtime extends longer than normal.

title: How to Tell If That Apple 'Threat Notification' Is Legit
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 14, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Yuliya Taba / iStock via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Threat actors are always finding ways to make their attacks seem more believable—often by using urgent security matters that push victims to act quickly—so you should always be skeptical of messages and notifications warning you that your device or account has been compromised. That said, if you receive a spyware warning from Apple via push notification, it's likely real, and you shouldn't ignore it. Apple's threat notification system is designed to alert individuals who have been targeted by mercenary spyware, such as Pegasus, which can silently infect devices and track everything a user does. Since 2021, the company has sent these alerts multiple times a year. In the vast majority of cases, those affected are in high-profile positions—such as politicians, journalists, and activists—that are at a high risk of being targeted. That means the average user is unlikely to ever receive one of these notifications, so it's important to understand how they work and be able to identify what's legitimate and what's not. Verify Apple threat notifications before taking actionAccording to Apple's support document, threat notifications are now being distributed via push notifications to affected users' iPhones. These alerts will appear on the Lock Screen and in Settings. Users will also receive an email alert to the address linked to their Apple Account sent from [[email protected]]. (Previously, Apple sent alerts via email and Messages.) Lock Screen alerts will have a red warning icon and read "Apple Threat Notification: Apple detected a mercenary spyware attack targeted at your iPhone. There are actions you can take now to help protect your data and your device."If you receive a push notification or an email that appears to be from Apple, you should take it seriously and also verify it in your device Settings and Apple Account dashboard, as scammers may try to capitalize on this by sending fake alerts that impersonate Apple. When you go to Settings on your iPhone, you'll see an Apple Threat Notification menu just below your main profile. Then, log into account.apple.com—there will be a banner at the top of the page labeled "Threat Notification" with a link to view additional details. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Legitimate threat notifications from Apple will never require you to click links, download files, install apps, or provide credentials by email or phone. If you're urged to do any of these things, it's a scam. You should be especially wary of security-related notifications if you're not a high-risk iPhone user who is likely to be targeted. That said, affected users are advised to follow Apple's recommended steps to protect themselves. This may include turning on Lockdown Mode, an OS-level security setting that severely limits iPhone features in order to block malicious actors from gaining access. If you receive an Apple threat notification, you can also contact Access Now's Digital Security Helpline, which is available 24/7, for assistance.

title: Why Microsoft Patch Tuesday Updates Suddenly Have So Many More Fixes
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 12, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Credit: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're a Windows user, you've hopefully installed regular Patch Tuesday updates from Microsoft, which address critical security vulnerabilities across the company's software. The last few months' worth of fixes have been especially important, as they've included a record number of bugs and a swath of zero-days that have been actively exploited or publicly disclosed. The August Patch Tuesday release this week is no different: The update fixes 400 flaws, including three zero-days. Compare that to March, when Microsoft issued patches for just 83 bugs in total (two of which were publicly disclosed zero-days). The seemingly sudden uptick in vulnerabilities and security fixes is due, in large part, to AI. AI is creating vulnerabilities (and discovering them)AI is playing both sides of the field when it comes to security. Threat actors are using AI to develop and deploy hacking tools more quickly and at scale, so more flaws may be more exploitable than before. This forces tech companies to respond more quickly as well. As ZDNET notes, companies that patch vulnerabilities during regular update cycles (like Patch Tuesday) now have to rush to address bugs sooner and may begin to shorten the time between updates, as Apple did earlier this summer.  While AI is helping to exploit vulnerabilities, it is also finding them so they can be fixed. Last month, Microsoft announced that AI has allowed its engineering teams to find and analyze a larger volume of potential flaws before they can be exploited. (The company noted that this also directly contributes to the increase in security updates included in Patch Tuesday). Google, too, is using AI to discover, triage, and fix security flaws in Chrome. It's worth noting that while AI is good at identifying vulnerabilities, it is far less effective at actually patching them—and may introduce more bugs along the way. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
As always, update your Windows device ASAPWindows users should ensure security updates are installed as soon as they're available to minimize the risk of active exploits. Patch Tuesday is released around 10 a.m. on the second Tuesday of the month, and you should receive them automatically. However, you can check the status under Start > Settings > Windows Update > Check for Windows updates.As BleepingComputer reports, the August security update addresses flaws across the following categories: 176 elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities, 11 security feature bypass vulnerabilities, 110 remote-code-execution vulnerabilities, 86 information disclosure vulnerabilities, 21 spoofing vulnerabilities, and 12 denial-of-service vulnerabilities. Forty-two of the bugs are rated "critical" and include remote code execution and elevation of privilege flaws.

title: Here’s What to Do Now That Microsoft Edge Is Phasing Out Ad Blockers
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 13, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Herstockart via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're a Microsoft Edge user, you will soon find that some older extensions—like uBlock Origin—no longer work. That's because Microsoft is following Google Chrome's lead in transitioning to the Manifest V3 extensions platform and disabling MV2 add-ons in the process. Edge is built on Google's Chromium engine, so the change isn't unexpected, but it does impact users who rely on older ad blockers. Microsoft is ending support for older Edge extensionsMicrosoft recently announced that it will begin turning MV2 extensions off by default over the next few months, and support for these add-ons will end completely for most users by the close of 2026. (The transition for enterprise is expected to be finalized in early 2027.) Microsoft notes that 95% of MV2 extensions on Edge have already moved to MV3, leaving fewer than 60 in the Edge Add-on store still on MV2. That includes uBlock Origin, which does have an MV3 version in uBlock Origin Lite, but the latter isn't as powerful as its predecessor and hides content rather than keeping it from loading in the first place. AdBlock, AdBlock Plus, and AdGuard are other MV3 alternatives with Edge versions, though they are not perfect replacements for uBlock Origin either thanks to restrictions on how MV3 ad blockers are able to filter content. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you want to retain the ad-blocking features you're used to, you can move away from Edge (and Chrome) to a browser that's not Chromium-based. The alternatives also tend to be pretty decent when it comes to privacy. One is Firefox, which runs on its own Gecko engine and still allows these older ad-block extensions, including uBlock Origin. DuckDuckGo and Brave both have built-in ad-blocking capabilities. Note that Opera, which is Chromium-based, has said the platform plans to continue MV2 support for now, but that may end eventually.

title: The Best Apps to Use After Gmail's 'Send As' Feature Goes Away
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 10, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: SOPA Images / Contributor / LightRocket via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you've been using Gmail to manage multiple email accounts, including third-party addresses, you'll soon have to find an alternative. Google is ending support for the "Send as" feature that allows users to send emails from external services like Hotmail, Yahoo, and Outlook as well as custom domains using their primary Gmail account. According to Google's support document, "Send as" will be discontinued in January 2027 for Gmail's web and mobile app interfaces. You'll still be able to add third-party accounts on mobile, meaning you can check your email on iOS or Android, but not send messages from those aliases. (Third-party accounts won't sync at all on the web.) Google is also eliminating "Gmailify," which allows you to add Gmail features like spam protection and inbox organization to third-party email accounts, as well as POP fetching on the web. Current users can continue to access these features until January 2027, but new users can no longer add them. This change does not affect "Send as" for other Gmail or Google Workspace accounts, nor does it impact Gmail access through third-party email clients like Outlook, Thunderbird, and Apple Mail if you already have these set up through IMAP or POP. You can also continue to forward messages from third-party providers to Gmail. One workaround is to send emails directly from the service provider's dedicated website or app. Obviously, managing multiple emails within Gmail is a way to streamline and consolidate disparate addresses into one interface, so this isn't the most convenient option if you have accounts across Outlook, Yahoo, and Google. Google also cautions against third-party tools and browser extensions that promise "Send as" functionality, as these require access to your credentials and may introduce security risks. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Switch to a desktop mail client insteadIf consolidation is your goal, your best bet is likely to switch to a desktop mail client and connect your third-party accounts via IMAP/SMTP. There are a handful of options that support multi-account setups, including Gmail addresses, and have "Send as" features. Our friends over at PCMag recommend the following email clients for most users: Apple Mail: For those in the Apple ecosystem, Apple Mail supports any email address and has solid privacy features.  Microsoft Outlook: If you're already a Microsoft 365 subscriber and use Outlook, this is an obvious choice. Outlook is also available for free as a standalone app. It works especially well for users who want the ability to separate messages into a Focused inbox. Mozilla Thunderbird: This is a free and open source platform from Mozilla, makers of Firefox. It works with all major email services, but there's currently no iOS app. These clients also have mobile apps (again, with the exception of Thunderbird on iOS) so you can keep the experience consistent across devices.

title: Watch Out for These Fake Fraud Alerts From Apple and Amazon
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 11, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Zooey Liao/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you get a security pop-up while you're browsing online alerting you to an unauthorized charge attached to one of your accounts, don't panic, and don't act impulsively. Scammers are currently using these alerts to impersonate Apple and Amazon support (and possibly others) to convince people that their accounts have been compromised and need to be verified to prevent further fraudulent activity. Naturally, this is just a ruse designed to gain access to your device or accounts, which will do far more damage than the fake alert itself. How the unauthorized charge scam worksThis campaign, described by Malwarebytes Labs, starts with a browser pop-up that appears on top of Apple's or Amazon's website. The alerts are designed to look like legitimate notifications and state that the user's Apple ID or Amazon account was recently used to make a $149.99 purchase. Targets are urged to call the support number listed—the same on both pop-ups—immediately to prevent further unauthorized activity. The scammer on the other end of the line may try to convince you to download a tool that provides remote access to your device, hand over credentials, or even pay a fee to protect your account. If you Google the number listed in this specific campaign, you'll find a fake Amazon support website ("amazonhelp[dot]support") set up by fraudsters to make the scheme look more legitimate—of course, the real Amazon customer service site is hosted on amazon.com. Other scam hallmarks present here include manufactured urgency, technical jargon, and a dollar amount that's just enough to get your attention but not so high that it seems like an obvious fake. Know how to identify a real fraudulent charge notificationFirst things first: no legitimate company will send you security alerts via browser pop-up. If there's an issue with your account, you may receive an in-app notification or an email, though you should always be wary of the latter, as it's also a common vector for scams. To confirm whether these alerts are real, log into your account by going directly to the website or app and check your message history or activity log. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's also worth noting that you won't dispute fraudulent charges with customer support over the phone. In fact, you're far more likely to deal with your bank or credit card issuer directly for this, and you may actually get a fraud notification from a financial institution first in the event of a suspicious purchase. Calling a number from a browser pop-up is not the way. Do not give out account information to anyone over the phone unless you have verified the number, such as by clicking through the company's app, and initiated the call yourself. Finally, these fake pop-ups may be the result of malicious ads, browser redirects, or compromised sites, all of which are used in phishing campaigns. If you're served one, exit the tab immediately and do not click or engage with it further.

title: Apple's iCloud Private Relay Can Actually Expose Your Real IP Address
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 6, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: picture alliance via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            As 404 Media reports, flaws in Apple’s web browser engine allow IP addresses to be revealed when they're supposed to be hidden.
                                            Web requests are made outside of the browser and the protections of Private Relay, meaning that websites that support passkeys can see users' real IP addresses
                                            If you want to keep your IP address hidden and your data encrypted across all apps and browsers on your device, you may want to consider a separate VPN.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you use iCloud Private Relay, Apple's paid IP address masking service, your internet browsing activity may not actually be private. As 404 Media reports, flaws in Apple’s web browser engine allow IP addresses to be revealed, either maliciously or incidentally, even when they're supposed to be hidden. How Private Relay is exposing IP addressesiCloud Private Relay, which is part of Apple's iCloud+ subscription, is supposed to keep both who you are and what sites you visit hidden when you are browsing in Safari. Without it, your network provider and the websites you view can see your IP address and DNS records, which can be used to track your location and browsing history over time. Private Relay is supposed to encrypt DNS records and generate a temporary IP address, keeping any single party, including Apple, from obtaining both. The issue, discovered by security researchers Talal Haj Bakry and Tommy Mysk, is related to how passkeys work. Web requests are made outside of the browser and the protections of Private Relay, meaning that websites that support passkeys can see users' real IP addresses. Obviously, this impacts Safari traffic, but researchers found the issue in Onion Browser, an iOS app that encrypts traffic through the Tor network. Both 404 Media and TechCrunch verified the issue in their own tests. The researchers stated that they informed Apple but haven't been given a timeline for when the vulnerability will be addressed. Apple is generally pretty good on privacy issues, but this isn't the first to arise in recent months. In July, "Hide My Email," the company's email masking service, was revealed to have a vulnerability that actually exposed users' real email addresses. Apple reportedly knew about it for over a year and claimed to have patched it—but it hadn't. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
While Private Relay can be a useful privacy tool—if it works as intended—it's not a true VPN (Virtual Private Network) because it only provides protection when browsing in Safari. If you want to keep your IP address hidden and your data encrypted across all apps and browsers on your device, you may want to consider a separate VPN service.

title: 10 Screenshot Hacks Every iPhone User Should Know
body:
Pranay Parab
                            
        
            Pranay Parab
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperiencePranay Parab is an independent tech journalist based in Mumbai, India. He covers tech for Lifehacker, and specializes in tutorials and in-depth features.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 14, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Adobe Stock
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        While the Mac has the best screenshot tools of any Apple device, it's not quite the same story on iPhone. Your iOS device is mostly restricted to built-in tools for taking screenshots and screen recordings, which makes it hard to bypass apps that block those features. Having said that, your iPhone's screenshot tool is anything but basic, supporting editing, annotations, and even extracting text from images. If you want to take better screenshots on iOS, these 10 hacks can help. 
Use AssistiveTouch to take screenshots without pressing any buttonsI've always found it unintuitive to take screenshots using hardware buttons on a device with a touchscreen. There are two easy ways to avoid pressing those buttons to take screenshots. The first one relies on a virtual Home button, which you can enable by going to Settings > Accessibility > Touch > AssistiveTouch. From here, enable AssistiveTouch to add a virtual Home button to your iPhone. Next, tap Customize Top Level Menu, then, if you're only interested in using this option for screenshots, reduce the number of icons from six to one by tapping the minus button. From here, tap the remaining icon on this settings page. Go to Device > Screenshot, and tap the blue checkmark in the top-right corner. The next time you tap the virtual Home button, your iPhone will immediately take a screenshot.The second method uses Back Tap, an iOS feature that triggers various actions when you physically tap the back of your iPhone. You can enable this by going to Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Back Tap. Select either Double Tap or Triple Tap, and go to Device > Screenshot. I recommend picking Triple Tap to avoid accidental screenshots. Once you enable this, tap the back of your phone thrice to take screenshots.Use this gesture to add calendar events directly from a screenshot
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
When someone sends you a screenshot of a ticket, or if you've saved an image that mentions a date or time, you can add it to your calendar with a hidden iOS feature. Once you open the screenshot, tap the small Live Text button in the bottom-right corner. (Its icon has three horizontal lines surrounded by dotted borders.) This will reveal a date or time in the bottom-left corner of the screenshot. Tap that button, and you'll see a new page where you can quickly add the event to your calendar. Sometimes, you may see a "More" button next to the identified date or time. This appears when there are multiple dates in a screenshot, and you can tap "More" to select the correct one for your calendar entry. Your iPhone can also identify flight numbers in screenshots and show you the current status of that flight.This is one of the best features for people who want to avoid piling up useless screenshots in their photo libraries. Once you capture a screenshot on your iPhone, tap the thumbnail to open the screenshot editor page, and tap the checkmark icon in the top-right corner. Here, you can select "Copy and Delete" to save the screenshot to your clipboard and delete it from your device. You can now paste it in other apps, such as Mail, Messages, or WhatsApp. Goodbye, clutter. Your iPhone comes with a powerful text extraction tool that lets you copy text from images. Just take a screenshot, tap the thumbnail in the bottom-left corner, and hit the Live Text button in the bottom-right corner. This tool instantly identifies all kinds of text in an image, and, from there, you can select and copy it easily.Hold the screen to draw symmetrical shapes in annotationsWhen I'm annotating a screenshot, I'll often draw a quick squiggle to highlight something to others who'll view it. Since I'm no Picasso, my attempts at drawing a circle (or any other shape) over an element in the screenshot look hopelessly amateur. Fortunately, iOS has a feature that allows you to turn your squiggles into regular shapes. Try this: Draw your best estimation of a circle, rectangle, square, or another shape on a screenshot. Immediately after, hold the screen, and iOS will convert your drawing into a neat symmetrical shape.Use opaque shapes to securely hide sensitive information in screenshots
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
I've seen way too many screenshots with poorly hidden bits of sensitive information. When people do this using an iPhone, they often use the pen tool or even the highlighter to hide email addresses, phone numbers, or names. It's surprisingly easy to bypass these methods for those in the know, leaving your info vulnerable. If you're trying to securely hide info in an image, use opaque shapes instead. It's a built-in tool on your iPhone that hides information thoroughly, and is much faster than scribbling over text hundreds of times. When you take a screenshot, open the image via its thumbnail, and tap the pen icon up top. Hit the + button in the bottom-right corner, and tap Add Shape. Choose any shape you like, and tap the first circle in the popover menu to add any color. This will make it an opaque shape. Now, drag this shape over sensitive information and save the image.Use this automation to delete unwanted screenshotsDeleting a bunch of screenshots by hand is a pain. However, you can use Apple's Shortcuts app to create an automation to do the job for you. The basic logic behind this automation is to find all photos that are screenshots taken in a specific time period, and delete them in one shot. For most people, this will work as a periodic cleanup tool that deletes recently taken screenshots. As an example, you can use it to delete all screenshots taken in the past 30 days. I've created a sample shortcut for you to follow. You can modify it to suit your needs, but if you use it as is, it'll find and delete all screenshots from the past month. It does ask for confirmation before deleting screenshots, and even after it's done, you can still recover photos from the Recently Deleted folder. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Disable thumbnails to stop accidental screenshotsThis might be how screenshots work on your iPhone: You take a screenshot, and the device shows a thumbnail in the bottom-left corner. This disappears in a few seconds, and saves the screenshot to your library. If you accidentally take a screenshot and don't tap the thumbnail fast enough, you'll have to manually delete the screenshot from your library. If this bothers you, then I recommend enabling full-screen screenshot previews. That way, the moment you take a screenshot (accidental or not), you'll see a preview, and you can decide if you want to keep the image. Apple has since changed this default, so there's a chance your screenshots now open in full-screen already. However, if your iPhone is still running with the thumbnail method, you can set this up by going to Settings > General > Screen Capture and enabling Full-Screen Previews.Enable microphone audio recording to create screencasts
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
In addition to screenshots, you can take screen recordings of your iPhone as well. There are many uses for this, but one of the best is to create a screencast. I use this often to help my parents solve tech problems. You can also add microphone audio to these screencasts to make them even more useful, and to avoid recording a voiceover separately. To do this, open Control Center by swiping down from the top-right corner of the screen. In case you don't see the screen recording button here, you can add it by tapping the + button in the top-left corner, and selecting Add a Control > Screen Recording.Hold the screen recording button until you see a pop-up menu. Tap the "Microphone Off" button, and it'll change to Microphone On. Tap Start Recording, wait for three seconds, and the screen recording will begin. You can now start speaking, and your voice will be a part of your screen recording.Use this shortcut to disable screen capture sounds and previewsIf you want to take screenshots with maximum efficiency, try Screenshot, a screenshot shortcut I found on Reddit. This shortcut bypasses all screenshot previews and capture sounds, and instantly saves your screenshot to a library of your choice. Once you install this shortcut, review its steps, and select an album for your screenshot. (It drops your screenshots in the Recents album by default, which may not be ideal for everyone.) From here, open Control Center, tap the + button, select Add a Control > Shortcut. Now select the Screenshot shortcut, and you're good to go. The next time you want to capture a screenshot as fast as possible, run this shortcut from the Control Center, and you'll notice that it's the least intrusive screenshot workflow. You could even link this shortcut to Back Tap gestures for even faster access.

    Table of Contents
    
        
        The JBL Go 5 is down to $44.95 from $54.95 on Amazon, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. At roughly four inches wide and just over half a pound, it is small enough to toss into a backpack, clip onto a bag, or keep on your desk without taking up much room. The upgraded IP68 rating also makes it a better travel companion than the Go 4, especially for beach days, hikes, or anywhere dust and water are likely to show up.
Battery life gets a modest improvement too, with JBL rating the Go 5 for up to eight hours of playback, or around 10 hours with Playtime Boost turned on. That should comfortably cover a day out, but it is not built for all-day-and-night listening. The same goes for volume. It gets reasonably loud for something this small, but it is better suited to a picnic table, bedroom, or a few people sitting nearby than covering a backyard party. Its front-facing driver also makes placement more important, since the sound is noticeably stronger when you are sitting in front of the speaker than off to either side.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
That said, the Go 5 does add a few conveniences that make it easier to live with—you can now play audio over USB-C, Bluetooth 6.0 brings LC3 codec support, and AirTouch lets you pair two Go 5 speakers for stereo simply by bringing them together. JBL’s companion app also gives you more control over the EQ if you want to tweak the sound. None of these upgrades dramatically change the listening experience compared with the Go 4, so owners of the older model do not have much reason to rush out and replace it. At $45, though, the Go 5 is the better buy for someone who wants a compact speaker with more durability, slightly longer battery life, and a few useful extras without moving up to a larger model.

        Back-to-school sales are aplenty this time of year, and one of the most popular deals in recent years comes from Apple, which offers eligible customers discounts and/or gift cards with the purchase of certain Apple devices for school use. This year, students, faculty, staff, and other eligible customers can get up to a $150 Apple Gift Card when buying a MacBook Pro, or $100 for a MacBook Air, iPad Air, or iPad Pro. You can read the full terms to see who is eligible, and the product list is below. The discount comes at a particularly opportune time: Apple recently raised prices on many of its devices by $100 or more—meaning you might be able to buy a MacBook today for what it effectively would have cost you back in June. And if you need more time, Apple extended its original Aug. 27 deadline until Sep. 24, giving us more time to shop for the right product.Here's the bad news: The new MacBook Neo isn't part of the deal, nor are the iPad mini, the  iPad (11th Generation), or any desktop Macs.
The Apple products must be purchased directly from Apple to get the gift card. At the moment, that could save you double, as Apple already offers educational discounts for eligible students purchasing many of these products—and that discount stacks with this gift card offer. You must use the gift card credit on Apple products, accessories, and apps, or subscription services like Apple Music and iCloud+ storage. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Who is eligible for the gift card offerIf you're a current or newly accepted higher-education student, a faculty or staff member at a higher-education institution, a parent purchasing on behalf of an eligible student, or an employee of a K-12 institution, you are eligible. As with the educational discount, you'll need to complete verification through UNiDAYS to get your gift card.

title: You Can Score a MacBook Neo for $599 in the Middle of 'RAMageddon'
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
            Deal pricing and availability subject to change after time of publication.
    
            Credit: Bloomberg / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        The global memory crisis—commonly referred to as RAMageddon—continues to make just about every piece of tech more expensive. Even Apple, a $4.5 trillion company, can't weather the markets without raising prices. What's more, Apple is struggling to produce enough Macs to meet demand, as you might discover if you try to buy a MacBook Air right now. While it's always a good idea to consider buying used tech, it now makes more sense than ever.As it happens, if you're in the market for Apple's "budget" Mac, the MacBook Neo, it's an excellent time to buy used. Apple originally released the MacBook Neo for $599, a fantastic price for a complete Mac experience. But since the RAM shortage, the company increased its starting price to $699—not bad, but certainly not as enticing an offer as it was at its release just five months ago. The MacBook Neo hits the Apple Refurbished Store But now, the MacBook Neo is officially available directly from Apple at its original $599 price point—as long as you buy it refurbished. But unlike buying a used piece of tech from a friend or a random outlet, Apple's refurbished store isn't unlike buying products new: The company says that it puts "Certified Refurbished" products through a "rigorous" refurbishment process, which includes testing, cleaning, and repackaging. Refurbished Apple products also have the same one-year limited warranty of new products, as well as a 14-day return policy, and you can purchase AppleCare if you so choose. As such, buying a MacBook Neo on the refurbished store should be just about the same experience as buying one new—except for the fact you have an additional $100 in your wallet. You get the same A18 Pro chip with 8GB of RAM, 13-inch display, 256GB SSD, and two USB ports (one USB 3 and one USB 2). If you want additional storage, as well as an embedded Touch ID sensor, you can upgrade to the 512GB model, also refurbished for $679.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
As tech gets more expensive, and companies make fewer products to sell, it makes sense to check out Apple's Refurbished Store for other devices, too. Just about every product category is represented here, to take a look before you buy a device at its full (and inflated) price.

title: Here's How Google's New 'Tap to Share' Android Feature Works
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 13, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Ivan-balvan via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google's new "Tap to Share" feature lets you share files and contact info by bringing your Android phones together.
                                            The company announced the new feature on Wednesday as part of Made by Google 2026.
                                            The feature is launching on Pixel 6 and newer, and will arrive soon on select Samsung Galaxy devices.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Google made a lot of announcements on Wednesday, all of them hours before its official Made by Google event. The company announced the new Pixel 11 series (including the Pixel 11 Pro Fold), the Galaxy Watch 5, and even the long-rumored Pixel Tag. There were so many announcements, one would be forgiven for assuming it was a hardware-only event. And yet, Google also revealed a number of software features, as well. The Pixel Watch received much of the attention here, as the company announced that its smartwatches will soon track trends in insulin resistance, blood pressure, and sleep habits, but the Pixel wasn't left out of the conversation either. In fact, Android devices across the board are getting one new feature that seems particularly useful: Tap to Share.Tap to Share appears to live up to its name. According to Google, all you need to do to use it is take your compatible Android device and place it near another compatible Android device. When you do, you'll pull up each other's contact cards, making it an easy way to share phone numbers, email addresses, and other contact info with someone new on Android. However, the feature isn't limited to digital business cards. You can also use it to share photos, videos, and other files from your Android to another. To use it, open the file in question, then launch the Share Sheet. Then, bring your phone close to the other user's. Now, instead of your contact cards, Android will send over your file. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
While Google might have announced this feature alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, it works with a lot of Google phones. The company says you'll be able to use Tap to Share on Pixel 6 and newer, which spans the entirety of Google's current supported Pixel devices. In addition, Google says Tap to Share is coming to some Samsung Galaxy phones, including the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Fold 8, and Flip 8, and will expand to even more devices by the end of 2026.   Tap to Share is, of course, similar to Apple's NameDrop feature on iOS, down to the contact card default. However, Android beat Apple to the punch originally. This is essentially an evolution of Android Beam, a discontinued feature that let you send data over NFC. And while the feature won't work with iPhones, Google and Apple do offer a quick sharing option for users trying to share from Android to iPhone, and vice versa.

title: Here's When Google Assistant Is Leaving Android
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 5, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Didem Mente/Anadolu via Getty Images)
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google Assistant is officially leaving Android. The company has started contacting existing users with the news.
                                            Google says that it will start removing Google Assistant from Android devices starting Sept. 4, though it will take a few weeks in total.
                                            This deprecation affects Android devices and Wear OS smartwatches, as well as some Android Auto cars.
                                            Google built-in cars, Google TV devices, and Google Home speakers and smart displays can continue using Google Assistant past Sept. 4.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        For the longest time, Google Assistant was the bot to beat. While those of us in the Apple ecosystem have struggled to get Siri to follow our commands, Google Assistant could answer almost any query you had. It led the charge on conversational AI, which let you ask a follow-up without needing to restate the original question in full. I've never been one to rely much on assistants, but I'll admit that I've wished Siri could be a bit more like Google Assistant over the years.Of course, Google Assistant isn't Google's assistant of choice these days. Since March of 2024, the company has let users swap out Google Assistant for Gemini, Google's flagship AI platform. Then, just one year later, the company officially replaced its popular bot with Gemini across its platforms and services. Google didn't outright kill off Google Assistant then and there; you've been able to use it if you wish, but it did say it would require Google Assistant at some point in 2025. 2025 has come and gone, and Google Assistant is still here, but that won't be the case for long.    Google Assistant has an official end-of-life dateAs reported by 9to5Google, Google Assistant will officially begin shutting down on Friday, Sept. 4. The company alerted some Google Assistant users via email, letting them know that Google Assistant is being discontinued, and Gemini, "our next-generation AI-powered assistant," is now the official Android assistant. On that date, Google says it will begin removing access to Google Assistant from devices, though it may take "a few weeks to reach everyone." That means you may still have access to Google Assistant through the third week in September, though you could lose access at any point. This Google Assistant end-of-life doesn't just apply to Android smartphones and tablets. Google says it will also revoke its legacy assistant from Wear OS watches, headphones, and Android Auto—at least when the feature is powered by the user's smartphone. Google says that "Google built-in" cars will still be able to use Google Assistant after Sept. 4.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Which devices will Google Assistant still work with?At this time, Google TV devices and Google Home speakers and smart displays still have access to Google Assistant. However, in some cases, it seems you cannot revert back to Google Assistant if you choose to use Gemini on your device.
